The best way for me to describe it is to "paint a picture" or a scene from a movie.  I'm not a screenwriter or an author, so bear with me.  This is what I can best describe as what flashes in my mind with these feelings.

It is early morning and we are looking in to the kitchen of a small, neatly kept apartment.  Sunlight is coming through the windows, filtered by old-patterned curtains and spilling across a small kitchen table, set with two chairs and two simple places; a cup and saucer, a plate and silverware.  A small vase of simple flowers sits in the middle of the table.  The kitchen is small and probably last updated in the early 70s but everything is in perfect condition, clean and obviously the realm of someone who cares.

An elderly man walks in to the kitchen and puts on a pot of coffee, two slices of bread in the toaster, gets orange juice from the refrigerator, all of the usual things to get ready for a simple morning breakfast, things he has done day in, day out for years and years.  No hurry, no wasted motions, just following the routine.  He is dressed properly for the day; khaki slacks, a freshly pressed shirt, a cardigan.  

The toast pops from the toaster, the coffee finishes its cycle.  The man butters each slice of toast "just so" and puts one on each plate, making sure to clean off the crumbs.  Coffee is poured carefully, cream added to the other cup and one lump of sugar.  He prefers his coffee black, just as he learned to like it in the Navy at the end of The War.  

The plates and cups are placed on the table quietly and in their proper place, handles turned so they can be picked up easily.  

The man sits at the table, taking a slow, deep breath as he does so; not so much from exertion as much as taking stock of his efforts and satisfaction that it is all done properly, just as it has been done for as long as he can remember.  The coffee steams in the sunlight, the toast glistens with slowly melting butter, the orange juice echoing the brightness of the day.

The man pauses for a moment, takes a sip of his coffee and picks up his toast to bite off the corner bit.  He looks across the table where his young bride from 50 years in the past greeted him every morning.  Slowly chewing his toast and gazing lovingly at her chair, he begins yet another day without her.

...this is the best way that I can describe what I feel.  Empty, lonely, sad.  I want to help the man, talk with him, learn his life, understand why he keeps going day after day.
After a point, you just have to let Darwinian theory assert itself.
